terms.definition: The complete set of chemical reactions occurring in a cell or organism.
A sequence of energy-requiring reactions that builds complex molecules from simpler ones.
A sequence of reactions that breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases usable energy.
A biological catalyst that increases reaction rate without being consumed by the reaction.
The region of an enzyme where specific substrates bind and catalysis occurs.
A reactant molecule that binds to an enzyme and is chemically changed.
The temporary association formed when a substrate is bound in an enzyme’s active site.
The minimum energy input needed for reactants to reach a transition state.
The model in which substrate binding changes active-site shape to promote catalysis.
The selective recognition and catalysis of particular substrates or reactions by an enzyme.
Reduction of enzyme activity when an inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site.
Reduction of enzyme activity by inhibitor binding away from the active site, lowering catalytic capacity.
A regulatory binding site distinct from the active site that changes protein activity when occupied.
A non-protein ion or molecule required for the activity of some enzymes.
An organic cofactor that transfers electrons, atoms, or functional groups during a reaction.
Control in which a pathway’s end product reduces activity of an earlier enzyme in that pathway.
The rate measured near the start of a reaction before major substrate depletion or product accumulation.
A set of pathways that transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP through redox reactions.
Loss of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule.
Gain of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule.
A coupled chemical process in which one reactant is oxidized and another is reduced.
An oxidized electron carrier that accepts two electrons and one proton to form NADH.
An oxidized electron carrier that accepts two electrons and two protons to form FADH₂.
The cytosolic pathway that converts one glucose to two pyruvate, with a small net yield of ATP and NADH.
Conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD⁺.
A cyclic mitochondrial pathway that oxidizes acetyl groups and produces carbon dioxide, reduced carriers, and ATP.
Direct formation of ATP by transferring a phosphate group from a phosphorylated substrate to ADP.
ATP production powered by electron transport and a proton gradient across a membrane.
A sequence of membrane carriers that transfers electrons through redox reactions and drives proton pumping.
Use of ion flow down an electrochemical gradient to power ATP synthesis.
Stored energy created by combined proton concentration and electrical gradients across a membrane.
A membrane enzyme that uses proton flow to phosphorylate ADP and produce ATP.
Respiration using oxygen as the final electron acceptor in an electron transport chain.
Respiration using a final electron acceptor other than oxygen in an electron transport chain.
An anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD⁺ by transferring electrons to an organic molecule without electron transport.
Regeneration of NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate to lactate after glycolysis.
The ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed during respiration.
Conversion of light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds, using carbon dioxide as a carbon source.
A molecule that absorbs selected wavelengths of light and can transfer excitation energy.
A green pigment whose excited electrons initiate light-dependent photosynthetic electron transfer.
A graph showing how strongly a pigment absorbs different wavelengths of light.
A graph showing the rate or effectiveness of a biological process at different light wavelengths.
A thylakoid pigment–protein complex containing an antenna and a reaction center.
Pigments and proteins that capture light energy and pass excitation to a photosystem reaction center.
The photosystem region where an excited chlorophyll transfers an electron to a primary acceptor.
Light-driven splitting of water that supplies electrons and releases protons and oxygen.
Thylakoid reactions that use light to produce ATP and reduced NADP while releasing oxygen.
Formation of ATP using a proton gradient generated by light-driven electron transport.
A cyclic set of stroma reactions that fixes carbon dioxide and produces carbohydrate precursors.
Incorporation of inorganic carbon dioxide into an organic molecule.
The five-carbon carbon-dioxide acceptor regenerated during the Calvin cycle.
The enzyme that catalyzes carbon dioxide addition to RuBP and can also react with oxygen.
The three-carbon product formed immediately after carbon dioxide fixation in the Calvin cycle.
A three-carbon sugar phosphate produced by Calvin-cycle reduction and used to build carbohydrates.
An environmental variable that restricts photosynthetic rate when it is furthest from its optimum.
A molecule that binds specifically to a receptor or other target protein.
A protein that binds a signal and initiates a cellular response.
Conversion of an external or internal signal into a sequence of cellular molecular events.
An extracellular signaling molecule that binds to a cell receptor.
A small intracellular molecule or ion that relays and often amplifies a receptor signal.
Communication by hormones carried through body fluids to target cells at distant locations.
Local communication in which a secreted signal acts on nearby target cells.
Communication in which a cell responds to a signal that it releases itself.
A signaling molecule released into circulation that regulates specific target cells bearing its receptor.
A water-soluble amino-acid polymer that usually signals through a receptor at the cell surface.
A cholesterol-derived lipid signal that commonly crosses membranes and binds an intracellular receptor.
A seven-pass membrane receptor that activates a guanine-nucleotide-binding protein after ligand binding.
A membrane receptor that activates kinase domains and phosphorylates tyrosines after ligand-induced association.
An enzyme that transfers a phosphate group from ATP to a target protein.
A sequence in which activated protein kinases phosphorylate downstream targets, relaying and amplifying a signal.
Increase in response strength when one activated component generates many active downstream molecules.
The electrical potential difference across a cell membrane caused by unequal ion distributions.
The stable negative membrane voltage of an unstimulated excitable cell.
An ATP-driven transporter that moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions into a cell.
A membrane pore that opens or closes in response to a change in membrane voltage.
A change that makes membrane potential less negative or more positive.
Return of membrane potential toward its resting value after depolarization.
A change that makes membrane potential more negative than the resting value.
A rapid, all-or-none reversal and restoration of membrane voltage that propagates along an excitable membrane.
The membrane voltage at which regenerative opening of voltage-gated channels triggers an action potential.
A time after an action potential when another is impossible or requires a stronger stimulus.
A multilayered insulating covering around an axon that increases conduction speed.
An unmyelinated axon gap rich in voltage-gated channels where an action potential is regenerated.
Rapid propagation in which action potentials are regenerated at successive nodes of a myelinated axon.
A junction where a neuron communicates with another cell electrically or chemically.
A chemical released from a neuron that binds receptors on a postsynaptic cell.
A graded membrane-voltage change in a target cell caused by synaptic input.
The narrow extracellular gap across which neurotransmitter diffuses at a chemical synapse.
A brain region that integrates neural and endocrine control of temperature, water balance, hunger, and other functions.
An endocrine gland linked to the hypothalamus that releases hormones regulating multiple target organs.
A cluster of endocrine cells in the pancreas that secretes hormones controlling blood glucose.
A pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake, use, and storage of glucose.
A pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose by promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production.
Formation of glycogen from glucose for storage.
Enzymatic breakdown of glycogen to release glucose units for metabolism or blood-glucose support.
An organ that filters blood, regulates fluid composition, and excretes nitrogenous wastes as urine.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: The microscopic functional unit of a kidney that filters blood and modifies filtrate into urine.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: A capillary tuft in a nephron where high pressure drives filtration into Bowman’s capsule.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: Pressure-driven movement of water and small solutes from glomerular blood into the nephron capsule.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: Transfer of needed substances from nephron filtrate back into the blood.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: A U-shaped nephron segment that establishes a medullary osmotic gradient for urine concentration.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: A hormone that increases water reabsorption by making kidney collecting ducts more permeable to water.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: A sensory cell that detects changes in the osmotic concentration of body fluids.
terms.sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 41 Osmotic Regulation and Excretion

terms.definition: A cell able to respond to a signal because it expresses the appropriate receptor.
A biological agent capable of causing disease in a host.
Rapid, non-specific defense mechanisms present before exposure to a particular pathogen.
Pathogen-specific defense that develops after antigen recognition and creates immunological memory.
A molecular structure specifically recognized by an antibody or lymphocyte receptor.
A secreted immunoglobulin that binds a specific antigen epitope.
An adaptive immune cell that can differentiate into antibody-secreting or memory cells after activation.
An activated B-cell descendant specialized to secrete large quantities of antibody.
A long-lived lymphocyte that responds rapidly after later exposure to its specific antigen.
A lymphocyte that coordinates immune responses by releasing cytokines after recognizing presented antigen.
A lymphocyte that kills infected or abnormal host cells displaying its specific antigen.
A cell that engulfs and digests particles, microbes, or cellular debris.
Uptake of a large particle or cell by membrane engulfment into an internal vesicle.
A localized innate response that increases blood flow, vascular permeability, and immune-cell recruitment.
A group of plasma proteins that enhances inflammation, phagocytosis, and destruction of microbes when activated.
Activation and proliferation of lymphocytes whose receptors bind a particular antigen.
Deliberate antigen exposure that induces protective adaptive immunity without causing the full disease.
Indirect protection that occurs when enough individuals are immune to reduce pathogen transmission.
The slower adaptive response following first exposure to a specific antigen.
The faster and usually stronger response following later exposure to the same antigen.

sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 45 Population and Community Ecology

terms.definition: Members of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
All populations of different species interacting within a defined area.
The number of individuals of a species per unit area or volume.
The largest population size an environment can sustain over time under stated conditions.
Population increase at a constant per-capita rate, producing a J-shaped curve under unlimited conditions.
Population growth that slows as density approaches carrying capacity, producing an S-shaped curve.
A population influence whose effect changes with population density, such as competition or disease.
A population influence whose effect is not determined by population density, such as a severe storm.
The rate at which births add individuals to a population.
The rate at which deaths remove individuals from a population.
Movement of individuals into a population from another location.
Movement of individuals out of a population to another location.
Estimation of abundance or distribution using counts within defined sample areas.
A line or belt along which organisms or environmental variables are sampled systematically.
Population estimation by marking an initial sample and measuring marked individuals in a later sample.
Selection in which every eligible location or individual has a known, unbiased chance of inclusion.
Directional change in community composition and ecosystem structure over time.
An early colonist able to establish in a bare or recently disturbed habitat.
A biological community together with the non-living environment with which it exchanges energy and matter.
A feeding position in a food chain or food web.
An autotroph that builds organic compounds from inorganic carbon using light or chemical energy.
An organism that obtains energy and carbon by feeding on other organisms or their products.
An organism, chiefly a bacterium or fungus, that externally digests dead organic matter and absorbs products.
An organism that ingests fragments of dead organic material and associated microbes.
A linear sequence showing transfers of biomass and energy through feeding.
A network of interconnected feeding relationships in a community.
A scaled diagram showing energy flow through successive trophic levels per area and time.
A scaled diagram showing dry organic mass at successive trophic levels for a stated area.
The total rate at which producers capture energy and store it in organic compounds.
The rate at which producer biomass accumulates after subtracting producers’ respiratory losses.
The rate of biomass or energy production per unit area or volume.
The percentage of energy or biomass at one trophic level transferred to the next.
The mass of living or recently living organic material in a stated area or trophic level.
Movement and chemical transformation of an element between organisms and abiotic reservoirs.
Transfers of carbon among the atmosphere, water, rocks, soils, and living organisms.
Transformations and transfers of nitrogen among atmospheric, inorganic, and organic forms.
Increase in a persistent substance’s concentration within one organism over time.
Increase in a persistent substance’s concentration at successively higher trophic levels.
